source_text: Τί τοῦτο λέγων; Τὴν παντελῆ ξηρασίαν καὶ ἐπίλειψιν τῶν ἀερίων ὑδάτων, δι' ὧν τῇ γῇ τὸ γόνιμον τῶν καρπῶν ἐνυπάρχει. Ὅταν οὖν ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ φέρεσθαι λέγῃ δρόσον ἢ ὑετὸν, περὶ ὑδάτων νοοῦμεν ὅσα τὴν ἄνω κατέχειν διατέτακται χώραν. Συναγομένων γὰρ τῶν ἀναθυμιάσεων περὶ τὸ ὕψος, καὶ πυκνουμένου τοῦ ἀέρος ταῖς ἐκ τῶν πνευμάτων πιλήσεσιν, ὅταν μὲν αἱ τέως ἀτμοειδῶς καὶ λεπτῶς ἐνεσπαρμέναι τῷ νέφει νοτίδες ἀλλήλαις προσχωρήσωσι, σταγόνες γίγνονται, τῷ βάρει τῶν συγκριθέντων φερόμεναι πρὸς τὸ κάτω· καὶ αὕτη ὑετοῦ γένεσις. Ὅταν δὲ τὸ ὑγρὸν ἐξαφρισθῇ, ταῖς βίαις τῶν ἀνέμων ἀνακοπὲν, εἶτα εἰς ἄκρον καταψυχθὲν ὅλον διόλου παγῇ, θραυομένου τοῦ νέφους, ἡ χιὼν καταφέρεται. Καὶ ὅλως, κατὰ τὸν αὐτὸν λόγον, ἔξεστί σοι ὁρᾶν πᾶσαν τοῦ ὑγροῦ τὴν φύσιν περὶ τὸν ὑπὲρ κεφαλῆς ἡμῶν ἀέρα συνισ ταμένην. Καὶ μηδεὶς τῇ περιεργίᾳ τῶν περὶ οὐρανοῦ φιλοσοφησάντων τὸ ἁπλοῦν καὶ ἀκατάσκευον τῶν πνευματικῶν λόγων παραβαλλέτω. Ὅσῳ γὰρ τὸ ἐν ταῖς σώφροσι κάλλος τοῦ ἑταιρικοῦ προτιμότερον, τοσοῦτον καὶ τῶν ἡμετέρων λόγων πρὸς τοὺς ἔξωθεν τὸ διάφορον. Οἱ μὲν γὰρ κατηναγκασμένον τὸ πιθανὸν τοῖς λόγοις ἐπάγουσιν· ἐνταῦθα δὲ γυμνὴ τεχνασμάτων ἡ ἀλήθεια πρόκειται. Καὶ τί δεῖ πράγματα ἔχειν ἡμᾶς τὸ ψευδὲς αὐτῶν διελέγχοντας, οἷς ἐξαρκεῖ τὰς αὐτῶν ἐκείνων βίβλους ἀλλήλαις ἀντιπαραθέντας ἐν ἡσυχίᾳ πολλῇ θεατὰς αὐτῶν τοῦ πολέμου καθῆσθαι; Οὔτε γὰρ ἀριθμῷ ἐλάττους, οὔτε ἀξιώματι ὑφειμένοι, πολυφωνίᾳ δὲ καὶ παρὰ πολὺ διαφέροντες πρὸς τὸν ἐναντίον αὐτοῖς ἀντικαθίστανται λόγον, οἱ τὸ πᾶν ἐκπυροῦσθαι λέγοντες, καὶ ἀναβιώσκεσθαι πάλιν ἐκ τῶν σπερματικῶν λόγων τῶν ἐναπομενόντων τοῖς ἐκπυρωθεῖσιν· ὅθεν καὶ ἀπείρους φθορὰς κόσμου καὶ παλιγγενεσίας εἰσάγουσιν. Ἀλλ' ἐκεῖνοι μὲν ἐφ' ἑκάτερα τῆς ἀληθείας ἀποσχιζόμενοι, ἔνθεν καὶ ἔνθεν τὰς ἐπὶ τὴν πλάνην ἑαυτοῖς ἐκτροπὰς ἐξευ ρίσκουσιν. 3.9 Ἡμῖν δὲ καὶ πρὸς τοὺς ἀπὸ τῆς Ἐκκλησίας ἐστί τις λόγος περὶ τῶν διακριθέντων ὑδάτων, οἳ προφάσει ἀναγωγῆς, καὶ νοημάτων ὑψηλοτέρων, εἰς ἀλληγορίας κατέφυγον, δυνάμεις λέγοντες πνευματικὰς καὶ ἀσωμάτους τροπικῶς ἐκ τῶν ὑδάτων σημαίνεσθαι· καὶ ἄνω μὲν ἐπὶ τοῦ στερεώματος μεμενηκέναι τὰς κρείττονας, κάτω δὲ τοῖς περιγείοις καὶ ὑλικοῖς τόποις προσαπομεῖναι τὰς πονηράς. Διὰ τοῦτο δὴ, φασὶ, καὶ τὰ ἐπάνω τῶν οὐρανῶν ὕδατα αἰνεῖν τὸν Θεόν· τουτέστι, τὰς ἀγαθὰς δυνάμεις ἀξίας οὔσας, διὰ καθαρότητα τοῦ ἡγεμονικοῦ, τὸν πρέποντα αἶνον ἀποδιδόναι τῷ κτίσαντι· τὰ δὲ ὑποκάτω τῶν οὐρανῶν ὕδατα τὰ πνευματικὰ εἶναι τῆς πονηρίας, ἀπὸ τοῦ κατὰ φύσιν ὕψους εἰς τὸ τῆς κακίας βάθος καταπεσόντα· ἅπερ ὡς ταραχώδη ὄντα καὶ στασιαστικὰ καὶ τοῖς θορύβοις τῶν παθῶν κυμαινόμενα, θάλασσαν ὠνομάσθαι διὰ τὸ εὐμετάβλητον καὶ ἄστατον τῶν κατὰ προαίρεσιν κινημάτων. Τοὺς δὴ τοιούτους λόγους ὡς ὀνειράτων συγκρίσεις καὶ γραώδεις μύθους ἀποπεμψάμενοι, τὸ ὕδωρ, ὕδωρ νοήσωμεν, καὶ τὴν διάκρισιν τὴν ὑπὸ τοῦ στερεώματος γενομένην, κατὰ τὴν ἀποδο θεῖσαν αἰτίαν δεξώμεθα. Καὶ μέντοι κἂν εἰς δοξολογίαν ποτὲ τοῦ κοινοῦ τῶν ὅλων Δεσπότου τὰ ὑπεράνω τῶν οὐρανῶν παραλαμβάνηται ὕδατα, οὐ λογικὴν αὐτὰ φύσιν παρὰ τοῦτο τιθέμεθα. Οὔτε γὰρ οἱ οὐρανοὶ ἔμψυχοι, ἐπειδὴ Διηγοῦνται δόξαν Θεοῦ· οὔτε τὸ στερέωμα ζῷόν ἐστιν αἰσθητικὸν, ἐπειδὴ Ἀναγγέλλει ποίησιν τῶν χειρῶν αὐτοῦ.
thought_title: Literal water above the firmament, not spiritual powers
orientation: Basil is explaining the waters above the firmament from Genesis 1:6-7 and rejecting allegorical readings that turn them into spiritual powers.
pass_a_gloss: What does he mean by this? The complete dryness and failure of the aerial waters, through which the fruitfulness of fruits exists in the earth. Whenever therefore he says dew or rain to be carried from heaven, we understand about waters as many as are ordered to occupy the upper region. For when the exhalations are gathered around the height, and the air is thickened by the compressions from the winds, whenever the moistures that until then have been scattered in the cloud in a vaporous and fine way come together with one another, drops come into being, carried downward by the weight of the combined parts; and this is the origin of rain. But whenever the moisture is made to foam, beaten back by the forces of the winds, then chilled to the extreme and frozen completely through, when the cloud is broken, the snow is carried down. And in general, according to the same principle, it is possible for you to see the whole nature of the moist element being constituted in the air above our head. And let no one compare the simple and unadorned character of the spiritual words with the over-curiosity of those who have philosophized about heaven. For as much as beauty among the chaste is more honored than that of a courtesan, so great is the difference of our words compared to those outside. For they bring to their words a forced persuasiveness; but here the truth lies open, naked of artifices. And why must we have trouble refuting their falsehood, for whom it is enough to set their own books against one another and in much quiet to sit as spectators of their war? For they are not fewer in number, nor inferior in dignity, but differing greatly in many-voicedness, they stand opposed to the opposing argument: those who say the universe is burned up, and comes to life again from the seminal principles remaining in the burned things; whence they also introduce endless destructions of the world and regenerations. But those men, splitting off from the truth on either side, find for themselves from here and from there the turnings aside into error. But for us there is also a certain argument against those from the Church about the separated waters, who under the pretext of anagogy and higher thoughts have fled to allegories, saying that spiritual and incorporeal powers are signified figuratively by the waters; and that the better ones have remained above on the firmament, but the wicked ones have remained below in the earthly and material places. For this reason, they say, the waters above the heavens praise God; that is, the good powers, being worthy, through purity of the governing part, render the fitting praise to the Creator; but the waters below the heavens are the spiritual powers of wickedness, fallen from the natural height into the depth of evil; which, being turbulent and factious and tossed by the disturbances of the passions, have been named sea because of the changeability and instability of their movements according to choice. Rejecting such arguments as comparisons of dreams and old wives' tales, let us understand water as water, and let us accept the separation made by the firmament according to the reason that has been given. And indeed even if the waters above the heavens are ever taken up for the doxology of the common Master of all things, we do not on this account posit a rational nature for them. For neither are the heavens ensouled, because they declare the glory of God; nor is the firmament a sentient living thing, because it announces the work of his hands.

choices.why: Basil distinguishes this technical term for higher spiritual interpretation from allegory; keeping the Greek loanword preserves the distinction he draws between the two pretexts.
The idiom γραώδεις μύθους is a standard pejorative for superstitious nonsense; the English idiom matches the dismissive force.

choices.english: let us understand water as water
choices.why: Basil's emphatic repetition of the noun is a rhetorical insistence on the literal sense; the English repetition preserves the force.
rejected: let us take water to be water
let us think of water as water

choices.why: The noun describes the discordant multiplicity of philosophical opinions; a literal rendering keeps the image of many voices in conflict.
This is a technical Stoic term; the standard English rendering preserves the philosophical register Basil is attacking.
The contrast is between the beauty of a chaste woman and that of a prostitute; 'courtesan' keeps the moral contrast without crude language.

bible_refs.note: οἱ οὐρανοὶ διηγοῦνται δόξαν Θεοῦ — 'the heavens declare the glory of God'
ἀναγγέλλει ποίησιν τῶν χειρῶν αὐτοῦ — 'announces the work of his hands'
τὰ ἐπάνω τῶν οὐρανῶν ὕδατα αἰνεῖν τὸν Θεόν — 'the waters above the heavens praise God'

pass_b_english: What does he mean by this? He means complete dryness and the failure of the waters in the air, through which the earth has its power to bear fruit. So when he says that dew or rain is carried from heaven, we understand it as the waters that have been appointed to occupy the upper region. For when the exhalations gather in the heights, and the air is compressed by the force of the winds, the moisture that until then was scattered through the cloud in vapor-like, fine particles draws together, and drops form, carried downward by the weight of what has collected—and this is how rain comes to be. But when the moisture is made to foam, beaten back by the violence of the winds, and then is chilled to the utmost and frozen through and through, the cloud breaks apart and snow falls down. In short, by the same principle you can observe the whole nature of moisture taking shape in the air above our heads.

And let no one compare the simple and unadorned character of the spiritual words with the over-curious speculations of those who have philosophized about the heavens. For as much as the beauty of a chaste woman is to be preferred to that of a courtesan, so great is the difference between our words and those from outside. Those men impose a forced plausibility on their arguments; here the truth lies open, stripped of artifice. And why should we trouble ourselves to refute their falsehood, when it is enough to set their own books against one another and sit quietly as spectators of their war? For they are neither fewer in number nor inferior in rank, but they stand opposed to one another with great many-voicedness, some saying that the universe is consumed by fire and comes to life again from the seminal principles that remain in the burned remains—which is how they introduce endless destructions of the world and rebirths. But those men, splitting away from the truth on both sides, discover for themselves the paths of error in every direction.

But we also have a word to address to those from the Church concerning the separated waters—those who, on the pretext of anagogy and higher thoughts, have fled to allegories, saying that spiritual and incorporeal powers are figuratively signified by the waters: that the better powers remained above on the firmament, while the evil ones stayed below in the earthly and material regions. For this reason, they say, the waters above the heavens praise God—that is, the good powers, being worthy through the purity of their governing part, render fitting praise to the Creator. But the waters below the heavens, they say, are the spiritual powers of wickedness, which fell from their natural height into the depth of evil. Because they are turbulent and rebellious and tossed by the disturbances of the passions, they were named 'sea' on account of the changeableness and instability of their movements of choice.

Let us send such arguments away as comparisons of dreams and old wives' tales, and let us understand water as water, and let us accept the separation made by the firmament according to the reason already given. And indeed, even if the waters above the heavens are sometimes taken up for the praise of the common Lord of all, we do not therefore assign them a rational nature. For the heavens are not ensouled just because they declare the glory of God (Psalm 18:2 LXX), nor is the firmament a living, perceiving creature just because it announces the work of his hands (Psalm 18:2 LXX).
notes: The source text contains 'συνισ ταμένην' with a line break in the middle of the word; it is read as συνισταμένην.
The source text contains 'ἐξευ ρίσκουσιν' with a line break; it is read as ἐξευρίσκουσιν.
The section marker '3.9' appears in the source text and is not part of Basil's prose.

problems.why: παραλαμβάνηται means 'taken/received/employed', not 'summoned'; the waters are taken/used for doxology, not summoned to it
problems.ruling: παραλαμβάνηται means 'taken/employed/used', not 'summoned'; waters are used for doxology, not called to it.

fixed: Changed 'summoned to the praise' to 'taken up for the praise' because παραλαμβάνηται means 'taken/received/employed', not 'summoned'.

last_rejected.quote: the moisture that until then was scattered through the cloud in vapor-like, fine particles draws together
last_rejected.source_quote: αἱ τέως ἀτμοειδῶς καὶ λεπτῶς ἐνεσπαρμέναι τῷ νέφει νοτίδες ἀλλήλαις προσχωρήσωσι
last_rejected.why: Subject is 'moisture-drops' (νοτίδες), not generic 'moisture'; verb is 'draw together to one another', not 'draws together' intransitively.
last_rejected.fix: the moisture-drops that until then were sown vapor-like and fine in the cloud draw together to one another
last_rejected.ruling: 'Moisture' renders νοτίδες acceptably; 'draws together' captures ἀλλήλαις προσχωρήσωσι adequately.

last_rejected.quote: some saying that the universe is consumed by fire
last_rejected.why: Greek has a definite article 'οἱ ... λέγοντες' = 'those who say'; English 'some saying' loses the specific reference back to the opposing philosophers.
last_rejected.fix: those who say that the universe is consumed by fire
last_rejected.ruling: 'Some saying' is normal English for οἱ λέγοντες in participial syntax; no reference is broken.

last_rejected.quote: failure of the waters in the air
last_rejected.why: ἐπίλειψις means 'failure to appear/scarcity' not 'failure' generally; 'failure of the waters' misrepresents the meteorological sense of waters ceasing/failing to come.
last_rejected.fix: scarcity of the waters in the air
last_rejected.ruling: ἐπίλειψις = 'failure/cessation/scarcity'; 'failure of waters' conveys the meteorological sense adequately.

last_rejected.quote: compressed by the force of the winds
last_rejected.source_quote: πυκνουμένου τοῦ ἀέρος ταῖς ἐκ τῶν πνευμάτων πιλήσεσιν
last_rejected.why: πιλήσεσιν means 'pressings/compressions' not 'force'; the air is thickened by compressions from winds, not compressed by wind-force.
last_rejected.fix: thickened by the compressions of the winds
last_rejected.ruling: πιλήσεσιν = 'pressings/compressions'; 'compressed by the force of winds' captures the sense adequately.

last_rejected.why: ἐξαφρίζομαι means 'to be converted into foam/froth' in meteorological context, i.e., water turning to foam-like snow, not 'made to foam' as active process.
last_rejected.ruling: ἐξαφρισθῇ = 'made to foam/froth'; passive 'made to foam' is a normal rendering, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.why: πολυφωνία here means 'disagreement/cacophony' (many conflicting voices), not a positive quality; they differ greatly in their conflicting claims.
last_rejected.ruling: πολυφωνίᾳ = 'many-voicedness'; the rendering conveys conflicting voices; a preference, not an error.

last_rejected.why: ἀναβιόσκομαι means 'to return to life/be revived' (intransitive middle), not active 'comes to life again' which obscures that the universe itself revives.
last_rejected.ruling: ἀναβιώσκεσθαι = 'come to life again/revive'; 'comes to life again' is a standard rendering.

last_rejected.why: ἐκπυρόω means 'to be consumed by fire/set on fire', not 'burned remains' (substantival misunderstanding); the seminal principles remain in things that have been fired/conflagrated.
last_rejected.ruling: τοῖς ἐκπυρωθεῖσιν = 'the burned things'; 'burned remains' is a reasonable paraphrase, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.quote: splitting away from the truth on both sides
last_rejected.why: ἐφ' ἑκάτερα means 'to either side of' (i.e., diverging in opposite directions from truth), not 'on both sides' as if truth were in middle; they veer off left and right.
last_rejected.fix: veering to either side of the truth
last_rejected.ruling: ἐφ' ἑκάτερα = 'on both sides'; 'on both sides of the truth' is a normal rendering of the idiom.

last_rejected.why: κατὰ προαίρεσιν means 'in accordance with deliberate choice/will', not 'of choice'; the instability belongs to movements that follow volition, not 'movements of choice'.
last_rejected.ruling: κατὰ προαίρεσιν = 'according to choice'; 'movements of choice' is a reasonable rendering, not a meaning change.

last_rejected.source_quote: Διηγοῦνται δόξαν Θεοῦ...Ἀναγγέλλει ποίησιν τῶν χειρῶν αὐτοῦ
last_rejected.why: These are Psalm 18:2 (LXX) = Hebrew Psalm 19:1, but the citations are split: first clause is verse 2a, second is verse 2b; both are verse 2 LXX, but the English marks both as 'Psalm 18:2 LXX' without distinguishing that two halves of same verse are cited.
last_rejected.ruling: Both citations are Psalm 18:2 LXX; marking both as such is correct; splitting a verse into two halves is not an error.
